nodes.text: I remember too that, when I had decided to enter a competition of theatrical verse, some *haruspex* [diviner from entrails] or other sent to ask me what fee I would give him to make me win; but I, detesting and abhorring those foul rites, replied that even if that crown were of undying gold, I would not allow a fly to be killed for my victory. For he was going to kill living creatures in his sacrifices, and by those honours he seemed set on inviting demons to support me. But this evil too I rejected not out of chastity toward you, God of my heart. For I did not know how to love you, I who knew how to think of nothing but bodily splendours. For does not a soul that sighs after such fictions commit fornication away from you, and trust in false things, and feed the winds? But of course I would not have [victims] sacrificed for me to demons, to whom by that superstition I was sacrificing myself. For what else is feeding the winds than feeding them, that is, by straying to be a pleasure and a laughing-stock to them?

There was at that time a shrewd man, very skilled in the art of medicine and most renowned in it, who as proconsul had with his own hand placed that crown of the contest on my unsound head, but not as a doctor. For of that disease you are the healer, you who resist the proud but give grace to the humble. Yet did you fail me even through that old man, or cease to heal my soul? For since I had become rather intimate with him and clung constantly and attentively to his conversation — for without refinement of words it was pleasant and weighty through the liveliness of its thoughts — when he learned from my talk that I was devoted to the books of the casters of nativities, he warned me kindly and like a father to throw them away and not to waste on that vanity the care and effort needed for useful things, saying that he had learned those things so well that in the early years of his life he had wanted to take up that profession as the means by which he would make his living, and that if he had understood Hippocrates, he could certainly have understood those writings as well; and yet he had afterwards abandoned them and taken up medicine for no other reason than that he had found them utterly false and, being a serious man, did not want to seek his living by deceiving people. “But you,” he said, “have rhetoric to support yourself among men, whereas you pursue this deception out of free interest, not because of the needs of your household. All the more, then, ought you to believe me about it, since I worked to learn it as thoroughly as one who meant to live by it alone.” When I asked him what cause, then, made many true things to be foretold from it, he answered as best he could that it was the work of chance, which is spread everywhere throughout the nature of things. For if, when someone happens to consult the pages of some poet who sang of and meant something quite different, a verse often came out wonderfully in harmony with the matter in hand, he said it was no wonder either if from a human soul, by some higher instinct, without its knowing what was happening in it, something sounded forth, not by art but by chance, that chimed with the affairs and deeds of the questioner.

So when I had heard and believed these things — for such was the man who had told them — all that resistance of mine gave way and collapsed, and first I tried to call Firminus himself back from that curiosity, telling him that, on inspecting his constellations, if I was to pronounce truly, I ought certainly to have seen in them parents foremost among their own people, a family noble in its own city, free birth, a respectable upbringing and a liberal education; but if that slave had consulted me on the same constellations — since they were his too — then, to tell him the truth as well, I ought in turn to have seen in them a most abject family, a servile condition and other things far removed from the former and far distant from them. And from the fact that, looking at the same things, I would say different things if I spoke truly — while if I said the same things, I would speak falsely — from this it is most surely inferred that what was said truly from consideration of the constellations was said not by art but by chance, and what was said falsely, not through lack of skill in the art but through the falsehood of chance.
